Judgment:
1.

The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the Pfa Act and Rules

. 
The accused no.4 is a partnership firm from both premises food article, that is, Dal Chana, was lifted for sampling.
Accused no. 1,2 and 3 are stated to be its partners, out of whom accused no. 1 was the vendor in whose presence the sample was taken.

2. As per the complaint, on 12.09.2000, food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) Arun Kumar and Virender Singh under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh.
G.R.Meena reached along with their staff at the premises of accused no. 4 at 458, Khari Baoli,
Delhi-110006 where accused no. 1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of Dal Chana from the vendor lying in open gunny bag (ready for In Re vs A-1) Manohar Singh on 28 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139439220/
1 sale) bearing no label declaration, to which he agreed.

sentences.text: The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI,
panchnama, etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 25.09.2000, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained rodent excreta along with dead and living insects.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by the FI.
It was found that accused no. 2 and 3 were also the partners of accused no. 4 firm in addition to accused no.1 vendor.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court by FI on 11.07.2001 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a),(b),(f),(h) and (l) of PFA Act, as punishable section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 11.07.2001.
The matter was then listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 Sh. Arun Kumar and PW-2 FI Virender Singh.
4. In the meanwhile, accused no. 1 expired and proceedings against him stood abated vide order dated 26.03.2009.

On the basis of pre-charge evidence, charge was framed against the accused no.4 firm on 24.08.2009 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a),(b) and (f) of PFA Act, to which it pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
At the same time, accused no. 2 and 3 were discharged by the court.
5. After framing the charge, the witnesses examined in pre-charge stage were recalled for further cross-examination in post charge stage.

Additionally, the complainant examined PW-3 Sh.
G.R.Meena in post charge stage.

6. PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 who were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings, deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 12.09.2000 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity,
expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 750 grams of Dal Chana (ready for sale) lying in an open gunny bag, thoroughly mixing it using a clean and dry jhaba,
dividing it into three parts by putting in three clean and dry sample bottles, separately sealing,
packing and marking the same and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, Notice as per Form-VI Ex.
PW-1/B and Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C.

On the next working day, that is 13.09.2000, one counterpart of sample along with Memo as per Form-VII were sent to Public Analyst (PA) for analysis vide PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/D and remaining two counterparts with copy of Memos were deposited with LHA/SDM vide receipt Ex. PW- 1/E.
PA report Ex. PW-1/F was received and upon direction of SDM/LHA, further investigation was carried out by PW-1.
PW-1 issued letter to the accused in response to which he received reply Ex. PW-1/G alongwith documents Ex. PW-1/H and Ex. PW-1/J.
They also received reply Ex. PW-1/K from the Sales Tax Department.

Thereafter, sanction Ex.
PW-1/L was taken from the Director PFA and after completion of the investigation, complaint Ex.

In Re vs A-1) Manohar Singh on 28 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139439220/
2 PW-1/M was filed in the court.
After this, intimation letter Ex. PW-1/N with copy of PA report was sent to the accused persons through registered post vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/O.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence counsel wherein they denied that the accused persons had been falsely implicated.
They however accepted that no insect was noticed by them through naked eyes at the time of sampling.
7. Statement of the accused no.4 (through its AR) under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 05.05.2012 wherein it denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
It accepted the proceedings dated 12.09.2000, though claimed that no efforts were made to join public witnesses and no price of sample was paid to the vendor.
It claimed that neither the firm nor its partners received the PA report.
It took defence that the method of taking sample was not proper as it should have been taken by quartering system and preservative should have been added.
It further claimed that its right under Section 13(2) PFA Act stood frustrated due to delay in filing the complaint.
It further stated that the report does not specify the identity of insects, whether larva, pupa or fully grown insects.

No defence evidence was however led by the accused no.4.
8.

Record shows that accused no. 4 continued to appear in the court through its AR as well as Ld.
Counsel but it was informed on 24.09.2013 that the said AR expired on 23.08.2013.
Court notices were issued to the accused no.4 but there was no representation on its behalf.

Subsequently, vide order dated 05.09.2016, the court directed to proceed against accused no. 4 firm ex-parte in view of Section 305 CrPC read with Section 17 of PFA Act because no person had been authorized by the said firm to represent it after the death of the previous AR and no coercive measures could be taken against such a fictitious entity.

Therefore, no arguments have been advanced on behalf of accused no.4.
9.

It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused no.4 firm beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that it has not been able to rebut the findings of the PA report dated 25.09.2000.
It is pointed out that the accused no.4 has failed to exercise its right under section 13(2) PFA Act and failed to get the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
10. Though no arguments have been advanced on behalf of accused no. 4, yet the record would reveal the defences sought to be taken by it.
It is the defence of accused no. 4 that the PA report and intimation letter were never served upon it and it was prevented from exercising its right under section 13(2) PFA Act.
It is further its defence that the nature / identity of the insects has not been given by the PA in the absence of which insect infestation cannot be established.

It is also claimed that there has been a delay of ten months in filing the complaint which also frustrated the right of the accused no.4 under Section 13(2) PFA Act.
11.
I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and have carefully perused the material available on record.

In Re vs A-1) Manohar Singh on 28 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139439220/
3 12.
Before proceeding with the merits of the case, it is to be understood that accused no. 4 is a partnership firm wherein its partners are no more facing the trial.
The matter is governed by Section 17 of the PFA Act which is pari materia to the Section 141 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
As per the Explanation (a) to Section 17, "company" means anybody corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals.
As per Explanation (b), "Director" in relation to a firm, means a partner in the firm.

13. Going by this provision, Section 17 lays down that in case of a company (which also includes a partnership firm), any person incharge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business can also be held liable in addition to the company.

Therefore, a partnership firm has also been given the status of a company for the purposes of Section 17 of PFA Act, despite the fact that it is otherwise not a separate and distinct legal entity as per the Companies Act.
Going by the language of Section 17, even a partnership firm can be proceeded against in the same manner as in case of a company.
Therefore, even if its partners are no more facing the trial, the matter can still proceed against the partnership firm.
14. Section 305 CrPC requires such a company (which includes a partnership firm in terms of Section 17 of PFA Act) to appoint a representative to participate in trial.
In the present case, one such representative was appointed by the firm but no other person was appointed after death of the earlier AR.
Obviously, the responsibility and prerogative to do so was of the firm itself and the court could not have directed it to necessarily appoint any person as its representative.
Since a firm is only a fictitious entity, no coercive measure could have been taken against the firm and the only course open to the court was to proceed against the firm in absentia.
In the present case, the firm has already been proceeded against ex-parte and therefore, it has to face the consequences accordingly.
15. On merits, it is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused no.4 is for violation of section 2(ia)(a),(b) and (f) of the PFA Act.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature, substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Under section 2(ia)(b) of PFA Act, it has to be established that the food article contained any substance affecting injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof.

Section 2(ia)(f) of PFA Act deals with situation where the article consists of any filthy, putrid, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or is insect infested or is otherwise unfit for human consumption.
16.
To begin with, it is seen that the accused has not exercised its right under section 13(2) PFA Act for getting the sample analysed through CFL.
For this, the stand has been that the PA report with intimation letter were never served upon it.

17. As per the scheme of the Act, under section 13(2) of the Act, after institution of prosecution against the accused, the LHA is required to forward a copy of the PA report to the accused,
informing that he /it may apply to the Court, within 10 days of receipt of report, for getting the sample (second counterpart) analysed by CFL.
Thus, this provision mandates sending of PA report to the accused by the LHA, after filing of the complaint.

It is a settled law that if the report is not so In Re vs A-1) Manohar Singh on 28 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139439220/
4 sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and would be fatal to the prosecution because this right cannot be allowed to be frustrated by the prosecution.
However, if the accused himself forgoes his right, then he cannot say that he was prejudiced.
18. At the outset, there is no merit in the contention that the PA report was not received by the accused no.4 firm.
PW-1 and PW-2 both deposed about sending the copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/N through registered post vide receipt Ex. PW-1/O.
The office file containing the documents had been produced at the time of evidence of PW-1.
Except raising a bald objection as to mode of proof of this document, such evidence has not been rebutted or questioned by the defence.

Not even a single suggestion was given to any of these witnesses that the postal receipt Ex. PW-1/O was a forged or fabricated document or that no such letter was sent or that it was sent at an incorrect address.
This document, which bears the stamp of the concerned post office clearly reveals the name and correct address of accused no. 4 firm at serial no. 0980 at which the registered letter was sent.
PW-1 was competent to prove this document as the document was sent through him in official capacity.
His statement, coupled with the fact that there is nothing in his cross examination to establish anything to the contrary, would be sufficient to prove that the letter was sent to the accused no.4.
If the accused was having any serious objection as to existence or correctness of this document, he could have summoned the record again and should have cross examine the witness on any such point.
But when the accused has remained silent throughout, it cannot take benefit on this count.
19. Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
It is not the case of the accused no.4 that the said letter Ex. PW-1/N was sent at an incorrect address.

No such stand has been taken by the accused at any stage of trial including prosecution evidence,
statement of accused or defence evidence.
Rather the reply Ex. PW-1/G given by accused no. 4 to the FI would reveal that the address at which the intimation letter was sent, was the correct and only address.

In such a position, when a letter had been sent through registered post at a correct and proper address, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.

The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered despite having been sent at a correct address through registered post.
But the accused no.4 has not led any evidence to this effect.
No attempt was made by it to summon the records of postal department to show as to whom the letter was delivered or if it remained undelivered.
There is no evidence to show that the letter was not delivered to the accused no.4 or any authorized person on its behalf.
Accused has not claimed that its office was at some other place or that it had shifted its work place at the relevant time.
Thus, accused no.4 has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
By not leading any evidence to support its stand, the version of the accused no.4 that the letter was not received by it, remains unsubstantiated.
Therefore, it has to be held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused no.4 in due course.
The accused no.4 cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things and claim that PA report was not received by it.
20. The commodity in the present case is Dal Chana which is food grain and has to be tested as per the standards prescribed for food grains.

The article is a standardize food article falling in Appendix In Re vs A-1) Manohar Singh on 28 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139439220/
5 B to the PFA Rules.
21.

The present case is based on the findings of PA as given in report Ex. PW-1/F that has found the presence of three dead and one living insect alongwith one piece of rodent excreta weighing 0.0122 gms in a sample counterpart of 250 gm.
There is nothing for the court to disbelieve the PA report wherein such findings have been given under the head "insect infestation".
Report of chemical expert is admissible in evidence under section 293 CrPC without formal examination of such expert.

As far as this report is concerned, the contents and findings therein have not been disputed by the defence, though it has been claimed at the trial that such findings are wrong on account of incorrect sampling methodology.
It is nowhere the defence of the accused that there was some mistake in the report.

Record rather shows that an application had infect been moved on behalf of the accused persons seeking to summon and examine the PA, but this application was withdrawn by the defence vide statement of Ld. Defence Counsel dated 25.07.2005.
Thus, despite the accused applying to examine the PA, he withdrew the application.
Thus, despite this option available to him under section 293 CrPC, so as to question the PA on her report and to seek any clarification, the accused chose to withdraw its application.
No explanation is given why the accused withdrew his application and deliberately forgave the opportunity to clarify the things by examining the PA who had analyzed the sample.
22. The PA would have been the best witness to have proved or disproved the stand of the prosecution and complainant.
She would have been a better person to establish if a sampling method was proper (as per the prosecution case) or improper (as per the defence version).
Only her evidence would have established or demolished the stand of the accused that the correct method to lift the sample was quartering system or addition of preservatives.
She would have also competent to explain if ten months period taken during investigation would have been fatal enough so as to frustrate the right of the accused under Section 13(2) PFA Act.
If the sample had been failed on any parameter which is prone to changes with the passage of time, the accused would have been given the benefit.
But where no such delay would have any effect on the parameters on which the sample was failed, no such delay would have frustrated the right of the accused.

Even if the complaint was filed after ten months, nothing had stopped the accused from sending the sample for analysis to CFL and to get its finding as to if there were living or dead insects therein or presence or absence of rodent excreta.
23. Similarly, the PA would have been able to even disclose the nature or identity of the insects detected by her.
It is to be noted that the PA report Ex. PW-1/F is only a final report given by the PA as per the format prescribed under the PFA Rules.
All the details, particulars, figures, calculations etc. are maintained separately by the office of PA, which can be easily summoned during the evidence of PA.
But despite this option, the accused chose not to proceed with his application.
He could have asked the PA to produce such record and to clarify if the insects were larva, pupa or fully grown insects.
In any case, all such insects would be a part of insect infestation.
Presence of three dead and one living insect in 250 gm of sample cannot be excluded from the meaning of "insect infestation" on hypothetical assumptions of the court.

The court cannot, without any reason, discard the opinion of a PA who is a food chemical expert and to substitute its own view without any basis and give a hypothetical finding that such presence of insects may not fall under the category of In Re vs A-1) Manohar Singh on 28 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139439220/
6 insect infestation.
The unrebutted PA report has to be honoured particularly when the accused itself chose not to cross examine her on any point.
24. All the PWs have corroborated the stand of each other on facts.
All deposed about attempt made to join public persons as witnesses.
All deposed about steps taken during sample proceedings.
There is no contradiction in their statements that can be said to be material enough so as to go to the root of the matter.
There is nothing to disbelieve them or to shake their credibility.
It is not a case of non-compliance of any Rule or procedure.
Rather the witnesses categorically deposed about compliance of due procedure and there is nothing in their cross-examination so as to attach any falsity to their version.
All the witnesses deposed about use of clean and dry jhaba and bottles.

As against this, there is no evidence in the form of testimony of any witness that any implement /
utensil / instrument was not clean and dry.
Not even a suggestion was given to any PW to the effect that there was any insect present on any such jhaba used or in any such bottle used.
If there were no insects in the sample, they would not have developed subsequently with the passage of time particularly when the bottles was fastened and sealed properly.
All the PWs have corroborated the testimony of each other on material counts and there is no contradiction in their version.
25. The fate of the case depends on quality of witnesses and not their quantity or designation or professions.
There is no rule of law that requires the evidence of food officials to be viewed with any suspicion.
What is required is that attempt is made to join public persons as witnesses as a matter of prudence.
The court is not oblivious of reluctance of public persons to join such legal proceedings that involves lengthy procedural formalities and strict future commitments.
But non joining of such witnesses would not negate the testimony of official witnesses when they are otherwise truthful and credit worthy and have withstood the test of cross-examination.
No motive has shown to exist giving them reason to depose falsely against the accused.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shriram Labhaya v. MCD [1948-1997 FAC (SC) 483] has categorically held that testimony of the Food Inspector alone,
if believed, is sufficient to convict the accused and there is no requirement of independent corroboration by public persons unless the testimony suffers from fatal inconsistencies.
No such inconsistency can be seen in this case.
No violation of any rule or provision has been pointed out by the defence.
26. Again, it is no defence available to the accused to claim that the three witnesses did not see any insect in the food article at the time of sampling.
It is to be understood that not all insects are visible to naked eyes and it is quite possible that the food officials did not notice any such insect at the time of sampling.

Despite any insect having come to notice to the food officials at the time of sampling,
the accused has virtually nothing to explain as to how the insects developed subsequently after two days after lifting the sample.
There is no allegation that the sample sent to the PA had been changed or altered in any manner.

After amendment in the PFA Act in 1973, it is not possible to change any such sample because the signatures of the accused are obtained on the bottle of the sample in a specific manner as per Section 11 of PFA Act and no such alteration can be done without the involvement of the accused.
27. It is not the defence of the accused that the food article was not meant for sale or was meant for any purpose other than sale for human consumption.

The food article would therefore be covered In Re vs A-1) Manohar Singh on 28 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139439220/
7 under PFA Act.
28.
No other stand has been taken by the accused no.4 at the trial.
29. The case in hand would be thus covered under section 2(ia)(a) as the accused no. 4 sold the food article which was not of the nature, substance of quality which it purported to be.
The case would also be covered under Section 2(ia)(f) as it was insect infested.

However, there is nothing on record to show that the food article contained any other substance which affected injuriously the nature,
substance of quality thereof so as to make out violation of Section 2(ia)(b).
Violation of section 2(ia)(f) is punishable under section 16(1A) and violation of section 2(ia)(a) is punishable under section 16(i)(a) of PFA Act.

But being graver offence, its conviction can be under section 16(1A) of PFA Act.
30.
Having said so, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused no.4 firm beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused no.4 had sold or caused to be sold through its vendor an adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (f) of PFA Act, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
31. Having said so, the accused no.4 firm is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1A) of the PFA Act.
32. Let the matter be listed for arguments on sentence.

Announced in the open court this 28th day of October 2016 ASHU GARG ACMM-II (New Delhi),
